records.sourceFile: Exploring the factors involved in being Ready to return to sport following a concussion.pdf

paper.citation: Caron JG, Cadotte G, Collict C, van Ierssel JJ, Podlog L. Exploring the Factors Involved in Being "Ready" to Return to Sport Following a Concussion. Clin J Sport Med. 2023;33(4):395-404.
paper.abstract: Interviews with 22 sport-injury stakeholders described physical, behavioral, psychological and social factors that they believed affect whether an athlete is ready to return to sport after a concussion. The authors argue that the graduated return-to-sport strategy in the Concussion in Sport Group consensus statement focuses mainly on physical factors and does not address the other factors that participants raised.
paper.tldr: Athletes, coaches and clinicians described readiness to return after concussion as more than symptoms and fitness, including avoidance, hesitant play, external pressure, mood and anxiety. These are interview themes rather than validated measures, so they show what to look for, not how to score it.
paper.methods: Qualitative study with individual semistructured Zoom interviews (average 72 minutes) of 22 stakeholders in contact and collision sports, analyzed by thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke with NVivo 12. Member reflections were sought from the participants, and 7 of 22 responded and agreed the results reflected their experience.
paper.findings: Participants described physical factors (concussion symptoms, 13/22; return to pre-injury fitness, 8/22), behavioral factors (avoiding contact, 4/22; malingering, 7/22; playing more passively, 9/22), psychological factors (cognitive appraisals, 22/22; mental health, 13/22; individual factors, 10/22) and social factors (external pressures, 21/22; social support, 11/22; isolation, 4/22; interactions between clinicians or coaches and the athlete, 8/22, or the athlete's teammates or roommates, 7/22). The authors conclude that these factors go beyond the physical emphasis of the graduated return-to-sport strategy.
paper.limitations: Only four athletes were interviewed, and most participants were university-educated and involved in Canadian ice hockey, so the findings may not transfer to other athletes or sports. Interviews were conducted by videoconference by two interviewers, and the counts describe how many participants raised each theme rather than prevalence in any population.
paper.practicalImplications: When judging readiness after a concussion, staff could look beyond symptoms and fitness to avoidance of contact, hesitant play, pressure from coaches, teammates or family, and mood or anxiety. Participants described athletes withholding information to be cleared and described asking directly, in private check-ins, about pressure and mood. These themes have not been validated as measures, so they should inform the clinical conversation rather than serve as clearance criteria.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches and staff could note hesitant play, avoidance of contact, or passive play in practice as signs that an athlete may not be fully ready. The study describes these signs but does not establish how to measure them.
paper.rtp: The study can inform how clinicians broaden their readiness assessment after concussion, but it does not validate any readiness test or set return-to-play timing or clearance criteria. Its findings are stakeholder perceptions, not measured outcomes, so they should not be used alone to make clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Factors Associated With Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Surgery.pdf

paper.citation: Webster KE, Nagelli CV, Hewett TE, Feller JA. Factors Associated With Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Surgery. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018:1-6.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study of 635 athletes after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction, assessed about 12 months after surgery, examined which factors were associated with psychological readiness to return to sport measured by the ACL-RSI. Self-reported knee symptoms and function were the strongest correlate, with younger age also contributing.
paper.tldr: Self-reported knee symptoms and function were the strongest factor linked to psychological readiness after ACL reconstruction. Only a quarter of this cohort had returned to competitive sport at about 12 months.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of athletes who had primary hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction by 1 of 3 surgeons at one private clinic between May 2011 and February 2013, were cleared to return to sport, and were recruited at their routine 12-month review. The ACL-RSI was the outcome. Predictors were sex, age, injury-to-surgery interval, preinjury sport frequency, KT-1000 laxity, single-leg hop limb symmetry index and IKDC subjective score. Univariate and stepwise multivariate linear regression were run for the full cohort and by return-to-competition status.
paper.findings: The ACL-RSI mean was 65 (SD 23). In univariate analysis for the full cohort, male sex (b = 5.8), younger age (b = -0.2), shorter injury-to-surgery interval (b = -0.1), higher preinjury sport frequency (b = 5.4), greater limb symmetry (b = 0.5) and higher IKDC score (b = 1.3) were associated with higher ACL-RSI scores. In the multivariate model, IKDC score (b = 1.2) and age (b = -0.3) remained significant and explained 37% of variance (r2 = 0.37). Laxity was not associated. Sex was significant only in the not-returned group in the univariate models (b = 5.1, P = .02).
paper.limitations: Causal relationships cannot be established from a cross-sectional design. The cohort was relatively homogeneous and came from one clinic. The abstract's statement that female patients have a more negative outlook rests on univariate results, since sex did not stay in the multivariate model.
paper.practicalImplications: Psychological readiness after ACL reconstruction tracks with how patients rate their knee symptoms and function, so staff can use the IKDC alongside the ACL-RSI when judging readiness. Because readiness was measured at one time point, the paper does not show that targeting interventions to female athletes would improve return rates.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not address performance training. Its findings relate to how athletes perceive their knee after surgery and whether they are ready to compete again, and it does not measure sport-specific performance.
paper.rtp: The study can inform the psychological side of return-to-sport discussions, showing that the ACL-RSI and IKDC are associated with each other at about 12 months. It cannot establish readiness criteria or safe return timing, and the authors note that high readiness does not show that return is safe.

records.sourceFile: Factors Associated With a Return to   Preinjury Level of Sport Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament   Reconstruction Surgery.pdf

paper.citation: Webster KE, McPherson AL, Hewett TE, Feller JA. Factors Associated With a Return to Preinjury Level of Sport Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Surgery. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019:1-6.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort of 222 patients who had primary ACL reconstruction and had returned to their preinjury sport was followed to a mean of 3 years to see who reported being back to their preinjury level of performance. About 61% did, and psychological readiness at 12 months was the strongest factor associated with that self-rating.
paper.tldr: Among athletes who had returned to sport after ACL reconstruction, about six in ten said 2 to 4 years later that they could perform as well as before injury. Psychological readiness measured at 12 months was the factor most linked to that self-rating, while age and sex were not.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort from one private clinic (surgery June 2014 to July 2016, 1 of 3 surgeons). Eligibility required a sport-related ACL injury, primary hamstring (98%) or patellar tendon (2%) reconstruction, no prior contralateral ACL injury, 12-month review data and a return to preinjury sport. At 12 months, age, sex, return to competition, KT-1000 laxity, limb symmetry (single and triple crossover hop), flexion and extension deficits, ACL-RSI, IKDC subjective score and Marx activity score were recorded. At a minimum of 2 years, return to performance was a self-reported yes or no answer, analysed with univariate and stepwise multivariate logistic regression.
paper.findings: Of 222 patients with complete data, 135 (61%) reported returning to preinjury performance (males 59%, females 63%). In univariate analysis, higher ACL-RSI (OR 1.03, P = .0001), limb symmetry (OR 1.03, P = .048), IKDC score (OR 1.03, P = .013) and Marx activity score (OR 1.07, P = .04) were associated with return to performance; age and sex were not. In the multivariate model only ACL-RSI remained significant (OR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.04), and it correctly classified 87% of those who returned to performance but only 26% of those who did not (63% overall).
paper.limitations: Return to performance was a single self-reported question, so it may not match objective performance, and the authors note that athletes can under- or overrate their performance. Follow-up was 2 to 4 years, the timing of return was not recorded, and 82% of the 272 patients who answered the performance question had complete data. The cohort came from one clinic and was homogeneous in sport and level, and factors not measured may matter.
paper.practicalImplications: Higher ACL-RSI scores at 12 months were associated with later self-rated return to preinjury performance among athletes who resumed sport, so the score is worth tracking alongside knee function. It should not be used on its own to predict an individual's outcome, since it identified only 26% of those who did not return to performance, and the observational design does not show that raising readiness scores restores performance.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not test training methods. It shows that athletes' own sense of readiness and confidence is associated with later perceived performance, which may matter when planning how athletes are reintegrated into training.
paper.rtp: This study informs the performance end of the return-to-sport continuum: about 61% of athletes who had already returned to sport rated their performance as back to preinjury level by 2 to 4 years. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria, time frames or overall return rates, because only returners were studied and the timing of return was not recorded.

records.sourceFile: Force and Power Testing During Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Rehabilitation - A World-Wide Survey of Current Practices.pdf

paper.citation: Compagnin A, Della Villa F, La Rosa G, Patterson S, Read P, Herrington L, et al. Force and Power Testing During Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Rehabilitation: A World-Wide Survey of Current Practices. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: International online survey of practitioners who assess patients after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, examining which force and power testing devices are used across rehabilitation stages and how the number and type of devices relate to self-perceived testing quality. Practitioners used a mean of 3.6 devices with wide variation in combinations. Force plates, isokinetic dynamometers, Nordic hamstring devices and hand-held dynamometers were associated with higher self-perceived testing quality.
paper.tldr: Practitioners test force and power after ACL reconstruction in very different ways, with 157 device combinations recorded in this survey. Those who used more devices, especially force plates and isokinetic dynamometers, rated their testing higher, but this is a self-report and does not show better patient outcomes.
paper.methods: Anonymous international online survey of 100 items in 12 sections, developed by an expert team, piloted in two rounds and open from April to July 2024, promoted by direct contact, conferences and social media. Closed responses were analysed descriptively, with Spearman correlation between device number and self-perceived testing quality, stepwise multiple regression, and trend tests across rehabilitation stages.
paper.findings: Of 1,154 respondents, 95.8% used multiple devices (mean 3.6 plus or minus 1.4), and 46.4% used device testing as criteria-based progression, 30.8% criteria- and time-based and 21.9% time-based only. Jump and hop devices without a force plate were used by 84.8%, hand-held dynamometers by 48.5%, isokinetic dynamometers by 45.7%, manual muscle testing by 44.7%, force plates by 35.7% and the Nordic hamstring device by 12.6%. Device number correlated weakly with self-perceived testing quality (rho=0.32, p<0.001), and force plates (coefficient 0.50), isokinetic dynamometers (0.44), the Nordic hamstring device (0.29) and hand-held dynamometers (0.21) were significant predictors (R2=0.21). Among the 1,072 respondents who did not rate their testing as excellent, equipment cost (77.2%), lack of space (34.2%) and managerial decisions (33.4%) were the most common barriers.
paper.limitations: Responses are self-reported in an anonymous survey with no response rate, and the authors state that question validity and reliability were not established. Three-quarters of respondents came from Europe and North America and most worked in private practice, which limits generalization. The survey was in English, device categories may have overlapped, and the authors note that engaged practitioners may be overrepresented, so testing quality may be overestimated.
paper.practicalImplications: Most surveyed practitioners used several devices, in 157 different combinations, and almost half used testing as criteria for progression, so local test batteries can be compared against this reported practice. Force plates and isokinetic dynamometers were associated with higher self-rated testing quality, but the survey does not show that they change rehabilitation decisions or outcomes. The authors advise caution when bodyweight, free-weight or machine tests estimate maximal strength from repetitions far from 1RM, and note that eccentric strength was assessed on the isokinetic dynamometer by only about 10% of the whole sample.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this is a rehabilitation testing survey, so its direct performance relevance is limited. It shows that jump and hop tests are the most common force and power measures after ACL reconstruction and that, among isokinetic dynamometer users, rate of force development and work were analysed by around a third, but it does not show that any device improves performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the survey describes testing used to guide progression and return-to-sport decisions after ACL reconstruction, with 46.4% using criteria-based testing and 21.9% relying on time alone. It does not validate any test, cut-off or decision rule, so it describes practice rather than supporting a specific return-to-sport standard.

records.sourceFile: Fundamentals of individual loading for strength training after knee injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Freiwald J, Javanmardi S, Hotfiel T, Engelhardt M, Rappelt L, Baumgart C. Fundamentals of individual loading for strength training after knee injuries. Sports Orthop Traumatol. 2023;39:368-377.
paper.abstract: This narrative review describes how strength training after knee trauma and surgery should be adapted from principles developed mainly in healthy athletes. It covers arthrogenic muscle inhibition, the neuromuscular basis of eccentric actions, biochemical and sensor-based monitoring, and psychological factors such as fear of pain. The authors propose an extended table of load parameters for orthopedic rehabilitation, including avoiding maximal (1RM) testing in injured athletes and keeping early acceleration and movement speed low.
paper.tldr: Strength training after a knee injury should be individualized, starting with low acceleration and loads, and maximal (1RM) testing should be avoided in injured athletes. The authors' load parameters are proposals, and the review does not test them against outcomes.
paper.methods: Narrative review and special-issue article. The text describes no literature search, selection criteria or quality appraisal. The authors draw on their own earlier work on knee injury and strength training, together with cited literature, to build an extended table of load parameters (intensity, volume, density, frequency, movement speed, range of motion and termination criteria) for orthopedic rehabilitation.
paper.findings: The review describes reduced neuromuscular activation after knee trauma from peripheral, spinal and central factors, and notes that eccentric actions need less activation to produce the same force. It advises against maximal (1RM) testing in injured athletes, against training to failure in early rehabilitation, and for low early acceleration and sensor-based monitoring. Table 2 lists general recovery times between sessions of about 72 to 84 hours for untrained people, about 48 hours for strength-trained athletes, and 24 to 48 hours for highly trained athletes.
paper.limitations: No search or appraisal is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The load parameters are proposals that the text does not test against rehabilitation outcomes, and the authors note that much of the underlying training research uses mostly healthy athletes. Claims such as eccentric training significantly reducing injury likelihood are given without effect sizes.
paper.practicalImplications: Start knee rehabilitation strength work with low acceleration, slow movement and low loads, and avoid 1RM testing and training to momentary muscular failure in the early phases, as the authors advise. Monitor joint pain, swelling, effusion and hyperthermia after sessions, and increase frequency and load gradually. Practice controlled movement reversal between concentric and eccentric actions, and keep deep squats out of rehabilitation in sports that do not need them.
paper.athleteDev: When returning an athlete from knee trauma, the authors suggest matching strength work to the demands of the sport and training the uninjured limbs and trunk more often with explosive work. The review gives no performance outcome data, so progression should be checked against the athlete's own tests.
paper.rtp: The review covers rehabilitation loading after knee injury and surgery, and notes that surgical, rehabilitation, social and psychological factors all affect return to sport. It gives no return-to-sport criteria or outcome data, so its load parameters should not be used as return-to-play clearance standards.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring injuries - A paradigm for return to play.pdf

paper.citation: Hoy MK, Stache S Jr, Roedl JB. Hamstring Injuries: A Paradigm for Return to Play. Semin Musculoskelet Radiol. 2024;28(2):119-129.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of hamstring injury anatomy, classification, MRI and ultrasound imaging, treatment, return-to-play decisions and prevention in athletes, with a focus on professional soccer and American football. It also covers the Nordic hamstring exercise and emerging machine learning models for RTP prediction.
paper.tldr: A radiology-led review that puts MRI grading, clinical tests and team context together when setting a return-to-play date after a hamstring injury. Imaging informs the decision but does not settle it alone.
paper.methods: Narrative review. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarize anatomy, injury classification, imaging, rehabilitation, UEFA and NFL data, and recent machine learning studies.
paper.findings: Grade 2 MRI injuries took on average about 6 more days to RTP than grade 1 injuries in a 255-injury UEFA cohort, as reported. Intramuscular tendon involvement was linked to longer time to full training (36 vs 24 days) and a higher reinjury rate (38% vs 12.5%) in English Premier League players. In the UEFA survey data, teams that used the Nordic hamstring exercise for all or most players had fewer hamstring injuries than teams that used it only for players with a current or prior injury.
paper.limitations: The review gives no search strategy, and it draws on cohort and survey data from particular leagues and clubs. Its prognostic correlations are group-level associations, not individual timelines, and the authors state that imaging does not capture all factors in RTP.
paper.practicalImplications: Use MRI grade and location as one input to RTP timing with clinical findings and sport-specific tests. When using the Nordic hamstring exercise for prevention, the cited UEFA survey data associate whole-squad use with fewer hamstring injuries than use limited to previously injured players.
paper.athleteDev: Use injury grade and location to set expectations for training return, and plan prevention programs for the whole squad, not only for players with a prior injury.
paper.rtp: Use MRI grade as one input to RTP timing, alongside clinical examination, strength and sport-specific tests. The review gives no validated RTP algorithm, so an MRI grade should not set a fixed return date.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring injuries, from the clinic to the field - A narrative review discussing exercise transfer.pdf

paper.citation: Vicens-Bordas J, Parvaneh Sarand A, Beato M, Buhmann R. Hamstring injuries, from the clinic to the field: a narrative review discussing exercise transfer. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2024. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Brief narrative review of hamstring rehabilitation and training exercise selection. It asks which exercises improve eccentric knee flexor torque during the swing phase of sprinting, when the hamstrings are exposed to high strain, and compares eccentric, isometric, flywheel, lumbopelvic, sprint and bounding approaches.
paper.tldr: Eccentric exercise, mainly the Nordic hamstring curl, is the only option with evidence of changes in running mechanics after training. Other methods are plausible but need kinematic and randomized trials.
paper.methods: Narrative review. No systematic search is described. The authors discuss hamstring demands during acceleration and high-speed running, the transfer principle, and the evidence for each exercise type from training, cross-sectional and biomechanical studies.
paper.findings: Nordic hamstring curl training increased eccentric hamstring strength by about 10 to 15% after 4 to 6 weeks in cited studies, and the one study that tested transfer linked the gains to larger terminal swing knee and hip moments. Flywheel training is described as more consistent with transfer principles but lacks kinematic studies. Lumbopelvic training reduced anterior pelvic tilt by about 5 degrees during swing in one study, but knee moments and injury risk were not shown to change, and bounding did not reduce injury incidence compared with a control group in one cluster RCT.
paper.limitations: The review gives no search strategy. Its transfer conclusions rest on very few kinematic studies, and several cited injury-reduction studies are small or pilot-scale. The authors note that some studies find no link between eccentric strength and injury risk.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose eccentric exercise, especially the Nordic hamstring curl, when the aim is to improve hamstring torque during running. Treat isometric, flywheel, lumbopelvic and bounding work as complements until kinematic or randomized evidence is available.
paper.athleteDev: Select eccentric exercise, especially the Nordic hamstring curl, when the aim is to improve hamstring torque during running. Use progressive sprinting to expose athletes to near-maximal speeds, and treat flywheel or isometric work as additions with less direct evidence.
paper.rtp: Use eccentric exercise and progressive high-speed running in late rehabilitation before return to competition. Individual muscle activity patterns may matter, but the review gives no validated EMG-based protocol, so exercise should not be individualized on that basis alone.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring muscle injury in the athlete - State of the art.pdf

paper.citation: Silvers-Granelli HJ, Cohen M, Espregueira-Mendes J, Mandelbaum B. Hamstring muscle injury in the athlete: state of the art. J ISAKOS. 2021;6:170-181.
paper.abstract: State-of-the-art review of hamstring injuries in athletes. It covers incidence and time loss across sports, risk factors, injury classification, MRI and ultrasound use, platelet-rich plasma, exercise-based rehabilitation, return-to-sport criteria and prevention programs. It reports support for eccentric and lengthening exercise and for the FIFA 11 and 11+ programs when compliance is adequate, and states that PRP use is not substantiated.
paper.tldr: Hamstring injuries remain common and recur often. Eccentric and lengthening exercise and the 11 and 11+ prevention programs have the best support, while PRP and MRI-based prediction of return to sport are not yet supported.
paper.methods: State-of-the-art review by four authors. No systematic search or appraisal method is described. The review covers epidemiology, mechanisms, risk factors, diagnosis, treatment, return to sport and prevention, with boxed key articles and practical tips.
paper.findings: In a cited meta-analysis, eccentric rehabilitation exercise significantly shortened time to return to sport but did not change recurrence risk. PRP trials gave conflicting results, and the authors do not consider PRP medically relevant at present. Prevention programs that include the Nordic hamstring exercise reduced hamstring injury rates, by up to 51% in a cited meta-analysis of 15 studies. MRI has not been shown to validly predict return to sport.
paper.limitations: The review is not systematic, and the authors describe evidence on several topics as limited or inconclusive, including PRP, fatigue, muscle imbalance and ethnicity. Some recommendations on lengthened-position exercise and running progression rest partly on mechanism.
paper.practicalImplications: Use classification, location and history to guide rehabilitation, combining eccentric and isometric hamstring work with a running progression. Include NHE or 11+ type programs in prevention, and monitor compliance, since the review reports that most professional soccer teams were not compliant.
paper.athleteDev: Plan running exposure and high-speed progression, and keep eccentric hamstring strength work in the season plan as a prevention program. Congested fixtures and fatigue are discussed as possible risks, but the review says the evidence does not yet directly link fatigue to injury.
paper.rtp: Use the review's return-to-sport domains (functional performance, strength, flexibility, pain and psychological confidence) rather than MRI alone. The review states that MRI does not reliably predict time to return or reinjury risk.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring rehabilitation in elite    track and field athletes - Applying the British Athletics Muscle Injury    Classification in clinical practice.pdf

paper.citation: Macdonald B, Mcaleer S, Kelly S, Chakraverty R, Johnston M, Pollock N. Hamstring rehabilitation in elite track and field athletes: applying the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification in clinical practice. Br J Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: This two-part clinical review describes how British Athletics manages hamstring injuries in elite track and field athletes. It sets out general principles (early structural diagnosis with MRI, a shared decision-making model, targeted training of the muscles and movements involved, eccentric and isometric loading, and attention to fatigue resistance and lumbo-pelvic control) and class-specific progressions for myofascial, muscle-tendon junction and intratendinous injuries. The authors propose this as a structured approach but present no quantitative outcome data.
paper.tldr: Match the rehabilitation plan to the BAMIC injury class, because myofascial injuries progress to running quickly while intratendinous injuries need a slower, longer tendon-loading progression. The approach is clinical reasoning from one national programme, not tested in a trial.
paper.methods: Clinical narrative review of the British Athletics hamstring rehabilitation approach. The authors describe general management principles, class-specific guidance, and example running and strength progressions in tables, drawing on cited literature and clinical practice. No formal literature search method or patient dataset is reported.
paper.findings: The paper reports no comparative or outcome data. It describes a diagnostic route with ultrasound and MRI within 72 hours, class-specific running and strength progressions, and return-to-full-training decisions based on clinical tests and shared team judgement. The authors state that their injury audit shows a marked reduction in previously published re-injury rates, but no figures are given.
paper.limitations: The approach comes from one elite track and field setting and may not transfer to sports with lower tendon or muscle-tendon demand, as the authors acknowledge. The class-specific progressions have not been tested prospectively, and the audit improvement is not quantified in the paper.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the BAMIC class to set the rehabilitation pace, with slower running progression and later eccentric loading for intratendinous (class c) injuries, which the authors estimate delays eccentric loading by about 3 weeks. Treat the progressions as a clinical framework to test locally, since the paper's evidence for them is expert reasoning.
paper.athleteDev: Use the injury class to guide the strength and running progression. High-load isometrics can precede eccentric work, and fatigue resistance and lumbo-pelvic control are included in the plan. The paper gives no performance outcome data.
paper.rtp: Return to full training is decided by clinical examination (range of movement, strength, palpation, Askling H-test), progression of high-intensity running, Nordbord strength at pre-injury level for MTJ and intratendinous injuries, and team shared decision-making, with repeat MRI as one input for intratendinous injuries. Table 3 gives approximate timeframes (about days 5-10 for 1a, days 14-28 for 2b, weeks 6-9 for 3c), but these are expert estimates, not outcome data, and no re-injury rates are reported.

paper.citation: Koc TA Jr, Bise CG, Neville C, Carreira D, Martin RL, McDonough CM. Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023. Clinical Practice Guidelines. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2023;53(12):CPG1-CPG39.
paper.abstract: This is the 2023 revision of the Academy of Orthopaedic Physical Therapy clinical practice guideline on heel pain and plantar fasciitis. It updates the physical therapy intervention recommendations from the 2014 revision, after systematic searches of MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library and PEDro from December 2012 to March 2023. The authors state that the search found no new literature that required fundamental changes to earlier recommendations on risk factors, diagnosis and examination.
paper.tldr: For plantar fasciitis, the guideline gives grade A support to manual therapy, plantar fascia and calf stretching, taping alongside other treatment, and 1 to 3 months of night splints for people with consistent first-step morning pain. It gives grade B support to resistance training for the foot and ankle and advises against orthoses used alone for short-term pain and against ultrasound to enhance stretching.
paper.methods: Clinical practice guideline based on systematic literature searches (MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library and PEDro; December 2012 to March 2023). Evidence was graded by level and recommendations were graded A to E. ESWT, corticosteroid injection and PRP were reviewed in scoping form only.
paper.findings: Grade A: manual therapy to lower extremity joints and soft tissue, plantar fascia-specific and gastrocnemius/soleus stretching, rigid or elastic taping with other treatment for short-term pain and function, night splints for 1 to 3 months in people with consistent first-step morning pain, and no ultrasound to enhance stretching. Grade B: no isolated orthoses for short-term pain relief, low-level laser as part of rehabilitation for short-term pain, therapeutic exercise including foot and ankle resistance training, and dry needling of trigger points. Grade C: orthoses combined with other treatment and phonophoresis with ketoprofen gel; grade D (conflicting evidence): manual therapy, stretching and orthoses may be used instead of electrotherapy, with iontophoresis or interferential current as second line; grade E: education and counseling on maintaining lean body mass.
paper.limitations: The recommendations depend on the trial evidence the panel reviewed, and the text does not report outcomes for athletes or sport-specific subgroups. The guideline is limited to interventions within physical therapy scope, so surgical, pharmacological and ESWT options are not graded.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing plantar heel pain in athletes can use the grades to choose among manual therapy, stretching, taping, night splints and resistance training for the foot and ankle. Orthoses should be combined with other treatment rather than used alone for short-term relief. Ultrasound should not be used to enhance stretching.
paper.athleteDev: Not directly applicable. The guideline addresses treatment of plantar fasciitis and does not report performance outcomes for athletes.
paper.rtp: The guideline can inform rehabilitation of plantar fasciitis, including loading through resistance training for the foot and ankle. It does not give return-to-sport criteria or timelines for athletes.

records.sourceFile: High speed runing during match-play before and after return from hamstring injury in professional soccer.pdf

paper.citation: Whiteley R, Gregson W, Bahr R, Tabben M, Chamari K, Lolli L, et al. High-speed running during match-play before and after return from hamstring injury in professional footballers. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022.
paper.abstract: Match tracking and medical data from 38 professional male players in the Qatar Stars League were analyzed for maximal speed, high-speed running and sprint distance before and after a first hamstring strain. Post-injury values were modestly lower, but the authors state the differences were within normal match-to-match variability for these measures.
paper.tldr: Professional players returning from a hamstring strain ran slightly less at high speed in matches, but the drop was within normal match-to-match variation. The finding describes match output after return and does not establish readiness or re-injury risk.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort analysis of multi-camera tracking data from 38 male outfield professionals (1,426 match observations) in one league, who played at least 45 minutes in at least 10 consecutive official matches as starters before and after their first hamstring injury in a calendar year (38 of 306 screened injuries). Multivariable random-effects generalized additive models compared pre- and post-injury maximal speed (km/h), high-speed running (>20 km/h) and sprint distance (>25 km/h), interpreted against match-to-match variability estimated from 265 players in one full season.
paper.findings: Post-injury minus pre-injury differences were -0.25 km/h for maximal speed (95% CI -0.38 to -0.12), -43 m for high-speed running (95% CI -56 to -30) and -22 m for sprint distance (95% CI -29 to -16). The authors state these could not be distinguished from the within-player match-to-match variation of 1.67 km/h, 102 m and 60 m. Median layoff was 14 days (IQR 4-21).
paper.limitations: Only players who met the 10-consecutive-start criteria were included, so the sample is likely a best-case group and results should not be extended to players who did not meet these criteria. The study covers one league, men only, and no standardized pre- and post-injury fitness tests, and it did not account for layoff length. The variability benchmark comes from league-wide data rather than an established anchor for meaningful change.
paper.practicalImplications: When players return from a hamstring injury, small drops in match maximal speed, high-speed running and sprint distance are expected and in this cohort sat within each player's normal match-to-match range. Match data alone did not capture capacity, so the authors recommend adding standardized high-speed running assessments during rehabilitation.
paper.athleteDev: For professional male players, returning from a hamstring strain was associated with small reductions in match speed and high-speed running that the authors judged within normal match-to-match variation. Coaches can use these values as context for expected match output after return, but the study does not set a target or threshold.
paper.rtp: This study can inform expectations for match running after return from hamstring strain in male professionals in one league. It cannot establish when a player is ready to return to play, or whether reaching high-speed running targets reduces re-injury, which the authors leave to future research.

records.sourceFile: High‐density electromyography activity in various hamstring exercises.pdf

paper.citation: Hegyi A, Csala D, Péter A, Finni T, Cronin NJ. High-density electromyography activity in various hamstring exercises. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2018.
paper.abstract: Nineteen amateur athletes without a history of hamstring injury performed nine hamstring exercises while high-density EMG recorded the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus. Activity patterns between the two muscles and along each muscle were exercise-dependent and, in some exercises, changed with contraction mode.
paper.tldr: Across nine common hamstring exercises, overall EMG activity varied widely, and the 45-degree hip extension was the only exercise with slightly higher biceps femoris long head than semitendinosus activity. Activity also differed between proximal, middle and distal regions in an exercise-specific way, but this single-session EMG study does not show training or injury effects.
paper.methods: Within-subject laboratory study in which 19 young male amateur athletes (soccer, Gaelic football, rugby) completed nine hamstring exercises at 12-repetition maximum in random order, with six repetitions each. Surface EMG was recorded from two 15-channel high-density arrays, normalized to maximal voluntary isometric contractions, and compared between muscles and between proximal, middle and distal regions for the eccentric and concentric phases.
paper.findings: Overall activity ranged from 17 to 54% MVIC (eccentric) and 32 to 83% (concentric) for the biceps femoris long head, and from 19 to 51% and 33 to 85% for the semitendinosus. Hip extension at 45 degrees was the only exercise with higher biceps femoris long head activity (d = 0.28 eccentric, 0.33 concentric; significant only in the concentric phase). Semitendinosus activity was lower distally than in the middle and proximal regions in bent-knee bridge, prone leg curl and slide leg curl (d = 0.53 to 1.20).
paper.limitations: The study had 19 men, all amateur and without hamstring injury history, and the authors state the results may not apply to injured or professional athletes. Surface EMG is prone to cross-talk, exercises used 12-repetition maximum loads, and no strength, adaptation or injury outcomes were measured. The abstract gives the biceps femoris long head regional range as 0.00 to 1.28 while the results give 0.02 to 1.28, and the results text reverses the eccentric and concentric order of the 45-degree hip extension effect sizes relative to Table 1 and the abstract; this review uses the table values.
paper.practicalImplications: When a specific hamstring emphasis is the goal, choose exercises by the muscle balance they produce. Hip extension at 45 degrees favored the biceps femoris long head, while straight-knee bridge, bent-knee bridge and one-leg Romanian deadlift showed no clear muscle difference in the eccentric phase. The authors suggest exercises with high overall hamstring activity, such as straight-knee bridge, upright hip extension and leg curls, may support adaptation, but this was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: For amateur soccer, Gaelic football and rugby players, hamstring exercises differed in overall activity and in how evenly they loaded the two muscles, so exercise selection can be matched to a muscle goal. These are single-session EMG patterns and do not show strength gains or reduced injury risk.
paper.rtp: This study can inform exercise selection in hamstring rehabilitation only as a hypothesis about muscle activity, since it tested healthy amateur players and no injured people. It cannot show which exercises speed recovery or reduce re-injury risk, which the authors recommend testing in future studies.
